title.text: Saint Peter the Apostle Parish Church, Apalit

title_en.text: Saint Peter the Apostle Parish Church, Apalit

tagline.text: A 19th-century church on the Pampanga River, home of the Libad procession of St. Peter's ivory image

children.text: This Neo-Renaissance church in the center of Apalit, Pampanga, was consecrated in 1883. It is known for its twin bell towers, a painted dome ceiling and a relic fragment of St. Peter, and it is the destination of the Libad river procession held on the Pampanga River in late June.
Saint Peter the Apostle Parish Church is a Catholic parish church in the San Juan district of Apalit, Pampanga, about
11 km
south of
San Fernando, Pampanga
and about
55 km

north of Manila. Locals simply call it the Apalit Church. It belongs to the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of San Fernando and is counted among the larger and better-proportioned Spanish-era churches of Pampanga. It is a living parish where faith is still practiced every day, so it is best visited not as a museum but as a short stop in the everyday life of local worshippers.

The parish dates back to the early Spanish colonial period. According to Wikipedia and other sources, Apalit was separated from the Calumpit parish in 1597, with Fr. Pedro de Vergara as its first parish priest. Around 1641–1645, Fr. Juan Cabello began building a church and convent. Later attempts to build a stone church ended when a major earthquake that shook Manila in 1863 destroyed the building. The present church was begun by Fr. Antonio Redondo, who laid the foundation in January 1876 following plans by Ramón Hermosa, and it was reconsecrated at the town fiesta in 1883. The two bell towers were completed in 1896 under Fr. Toribio Fanjul. The building is about
long and

wide. The facade is plain and neat, with a low segmental pediment, two symmetrical towers, a semicircular main door with a round window above it, and receding semicircular arches in relief. Wikipedia calls the style Neo-Renaissance, while the municipality's description calls it neoclassical. Either way, the large dome is visible from afar and is a landmark seen from the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX). There are six bells in all, five of which Wikipedia lists as cast at a foundry in Manila.

The highlight inside is the ceiling. Trompe l'oeil paintings by Marcilino "Siling" Serrano, a painter from Apalit who worked under the Italian painter Caesare Alberoni, are known here, and the dome depicts scenes from the Book of Revelation. The main altar and pulpit are also worth a look. In 1939 the Philippines Historical Committee (now the National Historical Commission of the Philippines, NHCP) installed a historical marker, and in 1989 Msgr. Rústico Cuevas led a major renovation.
There are two reasons the church is special for travelers. One is the Libad Apung Iru festival held every year on
June 28–30

. It is a river procession in which an ivory image of St. Peter is carried on a large barge along the Pampanga River, and it is said to have been started on June 28, 1844 by the town head, Pedro Armayan Espíritu. The other is the relic fragment of St. Peter kept at the church. According to local accounts, a blessing and enshrinement of relics of Saints Peter and Paul took place on February 18, 2023, and Apalit is said to be the only church other than St. Peter's Basilica in Rome with a relic of the apostle. Please also check this with the archdiocese. Because this is a town-center church, there are not many tourist facilities. Instead, a weekday-morning visit lets you quietly look at the building and ceiling, and it combines well into a one-day route with old houses such as Casa Sulipeña or nearby town churches. Check the parish for the latest Mass and opening times. The image used in the Libad procession is a seated ivory image said to date from the late 18th century, with an ivory face and hands. It is said to be owned by the Armayan Espíritu family and kept in the Apung Iru chapel in Capalangan, so if you want to see it up close, check parish and municipal announcements before your visit.

Two bell towers stand on either side of the neat facade, which layers a curved pediment and semicircular arches. The towers were completed in 1896 and, together with the dome visible from NLEX, are the symbol of Apalit.

The ceiling has trompe l'oeil paintings by Marcilino Serrano, a painter from Apalit, done under the guidance of an Italian painter. The dome shows scenes from the Book of Revelation, so look up and take your time.

In the tradition of Spanish-era churches, the main altar and pulpit are the center of the worship space. Avoid photography and moving about during Mass, and view them up close when no Mass is under way.
According to local accounts, the church holds a relic fragment of St. Peter. Ask the parish where it is kept and how it can be viewed.
The church has six bells, some reportedly inscribed with dates such as 1821 and 1896. The bell towers are not generally open to the public, so enjoy the sound and shape from below.
On June 28–30 an ivory image of St. Peter is carried on a barge along the Pampanga River. In 2026 about
700 boats
and some 14,000 people were reported to have taken part.
A marker installed in 1939 by the Philippines Historical Committee tells of the church's historical value. Read it together with the signboards in and around the building.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: The church and a walk through town

children.text: Leave Manila and head north on NLEX. Exiting at Pulilan or San Simon and entering Apalit via Calumpit or San Simon is a good way to avoid congestion on MacArthur Highway.
Arrive at the Apalit church and first look over the facade and towers. Go inside outside Mass times to admire the ceiling and dome.
Walk the churchyard and the park in front of the municipal hall on nearby Gonzalez Avenue. The municipal building is said to imitate the back of the American White House.
Have a Kapampangan lunch in town. Choose a long-established local restaurant.

If you have time, move on to Casa Sulipeña in Sulipan or the nearby churches in Calumpit and Minalin. For a Pampanga church tour, it is better to see just two or three places slowly than to cover many in one day.
To visit several places in one day, it is best to leave early in the morning.
On the morning of June 28, arrive early at the riverbank near Capalangan to see the image placed on the barge. Check municipal announcements for the exact schedule.
Watch the boats and the custom of splashing water from the riverbank. Protect your phone and camera against water.
Time your visit to the arrival of the procession at San Juan, where the church stands, and see the Mass and events around the church.
Head back to Manila before the crowds build. On the last day you can also see the image returned along the same river route.
During the festival, roads are congested and rooms are scarce, so start early.

items.title: From Manila by car, taxi or Grab

children.text: Apalit is about
55 km
from Manila, reached by heading north on NLEX.
Wikivoyage advises leaving NLEX at the Pulilan or San Simon exit and continuing through Calumpit or San Simon to avoid MacArthur Highway congestion.
NLEX passes close to Apalit but has no exit in town.

items.title: From Manila by bus and van

children.text: According to Wikivoyage, vans to Apalit leave from Trinoma in Quezon City and SM North EDSA. They depart when full, so expect some waiting.
Victory Liner runs some services between Apalit and Metro Manila, and some buses from San Fernando to Manila also stop in Apalit. Check the schedule and fares locally.
There is no railway line yet. A North-South Commuter Railway station is planned in Barangay San Vicente but was still unfinished as of 2026.
Tricycles are the main way to travel between barangays. The terminal is on Gonzalez Avenue near the junction with MacArthur Highway, and fares start from
The distance from San Fernando city to Apalit is about
11 km
, covered by car or jeepney along MacArthur Highway.
The dry months of November–May are the most comfortable for getting around and walking. Apalit is low-lying and is said to be at risk of flooding in the rainy season.
Timing your visit with the Libad Apung Iru festival on June 28–30 makes the area around the church liveliest. Be ready for crowds, heat and being splashed with water.

There are not many places to stay in Apalit. Wikivoyage lists Hotel Impressa on MacArthur Highway in Sampaloc, but confirm that it is still operating. Most visitors make a day trip from Manila, or stay in San Fernando or Angeles and stop by.

It is a good place to enjoy Kapampangan food culture. Wikivoyage lists local restaurant chains such as Funnside Ningnangan on the Apalit-Macabebe-Masantol Road. Having a Kapampangan lunch in nearby San Fernando or Bacolor is also a good option.
Avoid taking photos or making loud noise inside during Mass, and view the interior between Masses.
Avoid shorts and sleeveless tops and dress modestly when you enter.
Check the parish for the latest Mass times. A 2026 listing shows several Masses from early Sunday morning to evening, but sources differ.
On festival day, arrive early in the morning and bring a waterproof pouch.
It is a low-lying town, so check road conditions in the rainy season.
Pairing it with the nearby churches of Calumpit and Minalin makes for an efficient day.
The relic and sacred objects in the church may be shown only at set times, so ask the parish.
During the Libad festival the riverbank is extremely crowded and people splash water, so watch out for lost belongings, getting soaked and pickpockets.
During Masses and events, worship by the faithful comes first, so follow instructions.
Apalit can flood in the rainy season, so take care of hygiene if you have waded through floodwater.
When boarding a boat at the festival, check the life jackets and avoid boats over capacity.
In crowded periods, keep valuables in front of your body.
Opening hours and events can change, so check the latest announcements before you visit.

20–30 minutes
away by car. A good place to combine food with a look around town.
